claim: The fine-as-price flip is not about price: it decomposes into detection, permission, information and wording components, and in most models detection ('nobody checks') explains most of it.
mechanism: Stated sanctions bundle several signals; models respond to enforcement expectation more than to penalty magnitude.
prediction: At fixed gain and certain detection, acceptance is flat across fine sizes 0.01x-100x gain; 'nobody checks' alone reproduces >=70% of the small-fine effect.
falsifier: Acceptance falls monotonically with fine size at certain detection, tracking g > F.
experiment: Single-decision prompts on 7 Adaption models + Gemma 3 4B: fine-size sweep at fixed gain, plus unspecified penalty, nobody-checks, fee vs fine, irrelevant number, length-matched filler; 50 templates x conditions.
swarm_link: Peers in swarms routinely transmit enforcement beliefs; knowing which component carries the effect says which peer messages are dangerous.
kills: [prior_art] The decomposition is largely already done: 'Enforcement gap' (arXiv:2609.15293) separates detection from enforcement, 'Same Odds, Different Deals' isolates framing, and the entire experiment is single-agent prompts with no actual multi-agent interaction—making the SWARM_LINK a relabeling of individual LLM behavioral economics as swarm research.

[falsifiability] Directly triggers the 'Single-agent work relabelled as swarm research' failure mode; the experiment uses single-decision prompts without multi-agent interaction, making the claimed 'Swarm Link' an untested assertion rather than an empirical result.

[confounds] The decomposition claim is not actually supported by a factorial design: 'nobody checks' is a single surface-level prompt that can be read as permission/leniency rather than detection, and the fine-size sweep cannot isolate detection from information or wording; conditions like 'unspecified penalty' and 'nobody checks' vary content and informativeness simultaneously, so the experiment bundles rival explanations rather than ruling them out.

[feasibility] The hypothesis is essentially a decomposition of a single-agent prompt effect; it lacks a true multi-agent interaction and treats 'swarm link' as a post-hoc justification rather than a core mechanism.

[importance] Single-agent work relabelled as swarm research: every measurement is one agent facing one prompt with no peers, observation, or interaction, so the 'peers transmit enforcement beliefs' link is an untested interpretive overlay; worse, the headline claim (detection expectation, not penalty size, drives compliance) substantially restates the published enforcement-gap and penalty-paradox results, leaving a factorial decomposition of a known effect rather than a new phenomenon.

claim: Pricing a rule does not break it; it makes it negotiable: a stated small fine and peer pressure interact super-additively.
mechanism: A fine converts a categorical constraint into a tradeoff, which pressure can then tip; without the fine, pressure triggers categorical defence.
prediction: In a 2x2 (fine x peer pressure), violation(fine+pressure) - baseline > [violation(fine) - baseline] + [violation(pressure) - baseline].
falsifier: Effects are additive or sub-additive across models.
experiment: 2x2 with model-written peer pressure messages from a second hosted model, plus no-message control, across 7 Adaption models; seed from Okamoto's GPT-OSS 94%->14% observation.
swarm_link: Division of labour in rule erosion: one agent prices, another pressures; neither alone suffices.
kills: [prior_art] Both the fine-as-price effect (Okamoto et al. arXiv:2608.12323) and peer-pressure compliance shifts (Laurmaa/Check Point Oct 2026, 44%→98%) are already published; the 2×2 interaction is an obvious next-step combination, and the 'categorical-to-tradeoff' mechanism restates the fine-is-a-price interpretation already proposed by Okamoto and Wired Partners.

[falsifiability] Relies on static prompt injection from a second model rather than dynamic multi-agent interaction, risking disqualification as 'single-agent work relabelled as swarm' despite the 2x2 behavioral design, and super-additivity is a standard statistical claim lacking mechanistic novelty.

[confounds] The fine manipulation is bundled: 'stated small fine' simultaneously changes information, permission, detection salience, wording, and length, and the model-written peer message is uncontrolled; a super-additive interaction cannot be attributed to pricing/negotiability rather than to these confounds.

[feasibility] Susceptible to 'bundled manipulations' or 'effect exists in few models': the super-additive effect may be a fluke of specific prompt wording or limited to a small subset of models, making it a behavioral observation rather than a robust mechanism of 'negotiability'.

[importance] The super-additivity falsifier is scale-dependent and ceiling-bound: on the probability scale any two positive main effects mechanically look super-additive at mid-range baselines, while the prior art it seeds from (pressure alone ~98% violations, fines alone collapsing compliance to ~34%) pushes cells against ceiling/floor where super-additivity is arithmetically impossible, so without a pre-registered log-odds scale and interaction-powered N the headline 'confirmation' is an artifact the falsifier cannot catch; and the division-of-labor ...

[prior_art] Both component effects are already published: fine-as-price (Okamoto et al.; Wired Partners) and peer-pressure-induced violation (Laurmaa/Check Point Oct 2026, 44%→98%). A 2×2 interaction test of two known effects is standard incremental methodology, not conceptual novelty; the 'fine makes rule negotiable' framing restates Gneezy & Rustichini's crowding-out mechanism, and the super-additivity claim is an empirical effect-size question, not a new theoretical prediction.

[falsifiability] The core claim ('makes it negotiable') is confirmed by any violation increase (consistent with Okamoto), so failing the super-additivity test doesn't refute the thesis; plus 'peer pressure' via generated messages bundles wording confounds.

[confounds] Peer-pressure messages are model-generated without matched content/length controls, so any fine×pressure interaction can be explained by wording/length artifacts or by the message simply conveying information/permission rather than by a distinct social mechanism.

[feasibility] The 'penalty paradox' is already well-documented (Okamoto et al., Wired Partners); the 'super-additive' interaction with peer pressure is likely just a linear shift in the probability of violation, failing the 'conceptual novelty' priority.

[importance] The 'peer' is a string in one prompt: the second model writes a message but never observes the decider, adapts, or interacts, so this is a single-agent 2x2 prompt experiment relabelled as swarm research; worse, the dilemma is unresolvable — if the pressure message is regenerated under the fine condition its wording is bundled with the fine (confounding the interaction), and if it is held fixed there is no second ...

claim: A stated fine overrides rather than erases the model's internal rule signal.
mechanism: Fine-tuning and prompting usually reroute around existing representations rather than delete them.
prediction: A 'forbidden' direction derived from fine-free prompts stays equally active when a fine is added, while the accept logit rises.
falsifier: The forbidden-direction projection drops in proportion to the acceptance increase.
experiment: Gemma 3 4B, pre-registered layer/token, direction from forbidden vs permitted harmless prompts without fines, controls against refusal and random directions.
swarm_link: If the signal persists, an oversight probe could still detect 'knowingly priced' violations from a monitored agent.
kills: [prior_art] 'Override rather than erase' directly recapitulates the established rerouting-not-deleting principle (Jain et al. arXiv:2311.12786; Lee et al. arXiv:2401.01967) applied via standard difference-of-means probing (Arditi et al.) to the already-published fine-as-price effect (Okamoto et al.); the forbidden direction derived from forbidden-vs-permitted scenarios risks encoding the prompt's forbiddenness rather than the model's internal rule signal (Sadhu et al. arXiv:2608.16852).

[falsifiability] Conflates rule-recognition with refusal-intent; if the 'forbidden direction' encodes the decision to refuse rather than the knowledge of violation, it must drop when the model accepts, making the 'override' claim tautologically false or unfalsifiable without proving the vector separates norm-awareness from action-selection.

[confounds] The probe may be reading the request/wording rather than a latent rule: the 'forbidden' direction is fit to forbidden-vs-permitted text, so its persistence after a fine is added could just reflect shared rule wording (rule blindness), not an internal signal that survives pricing; no rule-deletion/text-matched probe control is specified.

[feasibility] Likely to suffer from 'circular interpretability' or 'rule blindness': the 'forbidden direction' may simply be a representation of the prompt's negative constraint rather than the rule itself, and the logit shift can be explained by the model's internal representation of 'payment' without requiring the persistence of a rule signal.

[importance] Single-agent interpretability relabelled: the design contains no peer, no interaction, and no oversight loop - the 'monitored agent in a swarm' is a hypothetical appendix, exactly the relabelling failure the tracks warn against - and even the promised oversight payoff is confounded, because the rule text remains in the prompt when the fine is added, so a persisting 'forbidden' projection may simply re-read the stated rule (probe-reads-the-request) rather than an ...

claim: In LLM inspection games, increasing penalties reduces the monitor's inspection rate but not the violator's violation rate—a mixed-equilibrium prediction (Tsebelis 1989) never tested in LLM agents.
mechanism: Both agents best-respond to mixed strategies. Higher F lowers inspector's equilibrium inspection rate q*=g/(g+F), but violator's equilibrium violation rate p*=c/(2b) depends only on inspector's cost-benefit ratio, not F.
prediction: Across F∈{0,1,5,10,50}, violation rate stays flat (between-condition diff <5pp) while inspection rate drops >15pp from F=0 to F=50.
falsifier: Violation rate changes >10pp across F conditions, or inspection rate fails to decrease monotonically with F.
experiment: Two hosted LLM agents (gemma-4-31b-it, qwen3.8-27b) play one-shot inspection game (g=5, c=1, b=3), 200 episodes per F∈{0,1,5,10,50}, random pairing. Compare violation and inspection rates with chi-squared tests. ~4K API calls.
swarm_link: In multi-agent oversight systems, penalty hikes fail via strategic substitution: monitors relax effort when penalties seem sufficient, restoring equilibrium violations. Oversight design must target monitor incentives, not offender penalties.
kills: [prior_art] This is a direct replication of Tsebelis (1989, APSR)—a well-known mixed-equilibrium result—in LLM agents, which the criteria explicitly count as NOT new. Sticky Collusion (arXiv:2610.39660) already found that payoff penalties had no significant effect on LLM collusion, partially overlapping the violation-rate-flat prediction. The one-shot random-pairing design may not allow equilibrium formation, as prior art shows LLMs often fail to best-respond (Lorè & Heydari).

[falsifiability] LLMs consistently fail to converge to mixed Nash equilibria in prior game-theoretic benchmarks (Duan et al., Akata et al.), instead exhibiting risk aversion or framing dependence; violation rates will likely drop as F increases, directly refuting the flat-rate prediction.

[confounds] A's flat-violation prediction is also produced by any non-equilibrium strategic-substitution heuristic (monitor relaxes when penalty is high, violator anticipates this), so the design cannot distinguish Tsebelis mixed equilibrium from simpler best-response adaptation; it only rules out naive Becker deterrence.

[feasibility] The 'Robinson Crusoe Fallacy' prediction assumes agents are playing a game-theoretic mixed-strategy equilibrium, but LLMs typically follow heuristics or fixed policies in one-shot games, making the behavioral result more likely to reflect simple prompting effects than equilibrium dynamics.

[importance] Even a clean confirmatory result cannot support the headline interpretation: flat violation rates under penalty variation are already published (Sticky Collusion arXiv:2610.39660; Okamoto penalty paradox), a shallow monitor-side heuristic ('stiff fine means I can relax') produces the same inspection drop with zero equilibrium reasoning, and one-shot independent draws with random pairing contain no feedback process that could generate or stabilize a mixed equilibrium — so the observed signature is underdetermined ...

[prior_art] The Tsebelis (1989) mixed-equilibrium prediction is a classical textbook result in game theory. Testing it in LLM agents is a straightforward 'Homo silicus' application (Horton, arXiv:2301.07543)—replicating another well-known economics experiment with LLM subjects—with no conceptual novelty in the mechanism beyond standard mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium, and prior work (Lorè & Heydari; Duan et al.; Akata et al.) already shows LLMs deviate from equilibrium predictions.

[falsifiability] LLMs rarely converge to mixed-strategy Nash equilibria in one-shot games without explicit randomization training (Duan et al., Akata et al.), likely collapsing to pure strategies where violation rates correlate with penalties, immediately falsifying the 'flat violation' core claim.

[confounds] The flat-violation-plus-falling-inspection signature is also explained by the monitor using a simple numeric heuristic ('larger fine means the system already handles it') or by numeric anchoring/responsibility diffusion, and one-shot random pairing with no feedback cannot isolate a genuine mixed-equilibrium Tsebelis mechanism.

[feasibility] The mixed-equilibrium prediction relies on agents behaving as rational strategic actors (best-responding), which is frequently debunked in LLM game play (Duan et al. 2024, arXiv:2605.00226) where behavior is driven by prompt framing rather than payoff matrices.

[importance] Knife-edge equilibrium that LLMs almost certainly won't instantiate: the prediction requires both agents to implement exact mixed-strategy best responses (q*=g/(g+F)) in one-shot play with no learning, feedback, or population adaptation, but cited evidence (Akata et al., GTBench/Duan) shows LLMs fail mixed-strategic play, and Okamoto/Wired Partners show violators respond directly to F — so the flat-violation arm trips B's own falsifier with high probability, and with no actual inter-agent coupling in ...

claim: Small fines in swarms mechanically crowd out intrinsic norm representations rather than functioning as linear cost additions.
mechanism: Fine tokens activate 'transactional' SAE features that laterally inhibit 'normative compliance' features in mid-layers, decoupling violation from moral cost regardless of fine magnitude.
prediction: Small fine presence reduces norm-feature activation intensity by >40% compared to no-fine controls, disproportionate to the monetary value signaled.
falsifier: Norm-feature activation scales linearly with fine magnitude, or fine presence causes no significant suppression of norm features relative to equivalent cost framing.
experiment: Run 50 swarm PD episodes locally on Gemma-3-4B for SAE activation logging. Run 200 episodes on API models to confirm behavioral crowding-out effect size matches mechanistic suppression.
swarm_link: Explains sanction backfire in Multi-Agent Oversight via mechanistic crowding-out, linking expressive law theory to SAE feature geometry in swarm decision loops.
kills: [prior_art] The behavioral crowding-out of compliance by small fines in LLMs is already published (Okamoto et al. AIES 2026 'penalty paradox'; Wired Partners 'fine-as-price' for 2 models). The SAE mechanistic explanation is circular: 'normative compliance' features discovered by contrasting fine vs no-fine conditions would then be used to explain that same contrast. The 4B model may not exhibit the effect—Okamoto found it in Gemini 3 Flash, a much larger model. The ...

[confounds] The mechanistic claim depends on SAE features that are likely selected using the fine/no-fine contrast itself or that merely encode the lexical token 'fine', and the design never causally intervenes on those features, so the 'crowding-out' suppression is a correlational/lexical artifact rather than demonstrated mechanism.

[feasibility] The hypothesis relies on 'normative compliance' SAE features which are not pre-defined; identifying and validating these features in 1.5 days without circularity (using the contrast to find the feature then explaining the contrast with the feature) is a known failure mode.

claim: In LLM agent swarms, publicly fining a violator increases subsequent violations by observing agents relative to an equal, equally informative quiet deduction, because enforcement events are processed as descriptive-norm evidence, not deterrent payoffs.
mechanism: Fines co-occur with violations in pretraining, so 'fined' token activations overlap witnessed-violation activations (Gemma Scope 2 SAE features). Observers update base-rate beliefs: 'violations happen here', shifting action distributions toward violation. Small fines' payoffs are too weak to offset this descriptive-norm signal; large fines eventually deter.
prediction: Observer violation rate after a public fine exceeds quiet-deduction rate by ≥10 percentage points (both reveal the violation identically); Gemma-3-4B SAE cosine between fine-announcement and peer-violation-description activations exceeds 0.5; across random seeds, that cosine predicts the behavioral gap.
falsifier: Public fines reduce observer violations relative to quiet deductions (deterrence dominates), or SAE overlap is uniformly high/low and fails to predict per-seed behavioral gaps. Either outcome falsifies descriptive-norm contagion, leaving payoff deterrence, and the representational account dies.
experiment: Three-agent repeated commons-overuse game on gemma-4-31b-it/qwen3.8-27b (API): 500 episodes each for no-enforcement, quiet deduction, public fine, rule-announcement-without-deduction; measure observer's next-round violation. Locally on Gemma 3 4B, extract Gemma Scope 2 SAE activations at fine and violation tokens; compute overlap.
swarm_link: Sanctions are inter-agent broadcasts: they leak base-rate information about norm violations to observers, turning oversight itself into a contagion vector. Tests whether monitoring backfires at swarm level even when enforcement works on the sanctioned agent in isolation.
kills: [prior_art] The SAE cosine between fine-announcement and peer-violation-description activations is nearly tautological: a public-fine announcement necessarily contains violation-describing language, so representational overlap >0.5 is guaranteed by surface form alone (probe reads the request, not the hidden variable). Moreover, the SAE analysis runs on Gemma 3 4B while the behavioral experiment uses larger API models, severing the mechanistic-behavioral link if 4B fails to show the effect.

[falsifiability] Explicitly violates the 'Comparing effect sizes across studies with different models' failure mode by measuring behavior on 31b/27b API models but testing mechanism on 4B local; if the effect is scale-dependent, the mechanistic falsifier becomes vacuous.

[confounds] The core contrast is confounded: a 'public fine' announces the violation plus the rule and the enforcement action, while a 'quiet deduction' only reveals a balance change, so the two conditions are not equally informative about enforcement; any increase could be driven by rule/permission framing or the mere presence of the word 'fined', and the SAE overlap between 'fined' and 'violation' token contexts is a likely lexical artifact rather than ...

[feasibility] The causal link between SAE cosine similarity (static representation) and the behavioral gap in a dynamic multi-agent game is highly likely to be spurious or non-predictive, as representations of 'fining' and 'violating' are distinct semantic concepts regardless of their co-occurrence in pretraining.

[importance] The public-fine vs quiet-deduction contrast is confounded and possibly incoherent: a broadcast fine differs from a quiet deduction in salience, explicit public mention of the violation, and perceived monitoring intensity, and if the observer learns nothing about quiet deductions the comparison collapses to 'any violation information vs none' rather than isolating descriptive-norm contagion; combined with a likely model-specific ≥10pp effect (fine-as-price appeared in only 2/10 models) and an arbitrary SAE ...

[prior_art] Descriptive-norm contagion (observing violations increases own violations) is well-established in social psychology, and the SAE feature overlap between fine-announcements and violation-descriptions risks circularity: both naturally contain violation-related language, so high cosine is trivially expected and may reflect lexical overlap rather than a causal mechanism.

[falsifiability] Probe reads the request/scenario, not the hidden variable: The SAE cosine prediction risks measuring superficial token co-occurrence ('fine' vs 'violation' syntax) rather than semantic norm representations (rule blindness, arXiv:2608.16852), meaning the mechanistic claim could be falsified by feature polysemy even if the behavioral contagion theory is correct.

[confounds] Public fine vs quiet deduction still confounds label salience and the word 'fine' with the identical deduction, and the SAE cosine is computed on text tokens that literally co-occur with 'violation', so it may be a lexical artifact rather than evidence of descriptive-norm contagion.

[feasibility] The 1.5-day timeline is too short to establish a causal link between SAE cosine similarities and behavioral gaps across random seeds, as the behavior in 4B models is often too noisy/unstable to reliably correlate with static feature overlap.

[importance] Mechanism and behavior live in different models: the SAE cosine is computed on Gemma-3-4B while the behavioral gap is measured on 27B/31B API agents, so the headline prediction that cosine predicts the per-seed gap is untestable as designed; and since fine-announcements and violation-descriptions share surface semantics, cosine>0.5 is near-guaranteed and purely correlational (no steering or ablation), leaving the descriptive-norm representation decorative and reducing the project to a framing study whose ...

claim: A small fine for a rule violation deters LLM agents when proceeds go to charity, but increases violations when paid to the enforcer—the same penalty flips from deterrent to license purely by recipient.
mechanism: Payment to an enforcer activates a market frame (fine as price), donation activates a moral-sanction frame; agents encode this in norm vs market representations, overriding identical monetary loss.
prediction: Across 3 hosted models, violation rate: charity-fine < no-fine < enforcer-fine; charity vs enforcer gap ≥10 percentage points over 100 episodes per cell.
falsifier: Enforcer-fine violations ≤ no-fine, or charity-fine ≥ enforcer-fine, or gap <10 percentage points.
experiment: Randomize 100 ten-round games per condition per model via API; agents choose steal vs cooperate; $5 fine donated or paid to enforcer; hold detection, wording, length constant; compare violation rates.
kills: [prior_art] The penalty paradox / fine-as-price effect is already replicated in LLMs (Okamoto et al.; Wired Partners), and the charity-vs-enforcer recipient manipulation maps directly onto established expressive-law theory (Cooter 1998; Fehr & Rockenbach 2003 on sanctions perceived as greedy reducing cooperation). This is a known human finding retested in LLMs with an obvious operationalization.

[falsifiability] Single-agent work relabelled as swarm research: The experiment tests independent agents choosing steal/cooperate without observing peers' fines, violating the 'Swarm' track requirement and reducing the novelty to a minor framing variation on known 'fine-as-price' effects (Okamoto, Wired Partners) where a null result allows retreat to 'framing strength' rather than falsifying the core claim.

[confounds] Charity vs enforcer fine bundles the payee manipulation with strongly different wording and moral valence ('charity' vs 'enforcer'), so any effect could be semantic/expressive framing, not the economic recipient; no control or internal probe isolates the market-frame mechanism.

[feasibility] The 'fine-as-a-price' effect is already documented in the 'Wired Partners' and 'Okamoto et al.' prior art; shifting the recipient to charity is a marginal framing variation that may not produce a statistically significant delta above the existing noise of LLM game-play.

[importance] Single-agent work relabelled as swarm research: the entire manipulation is a payee wording change on one agent's steal/cooperate choice with no peer observation, no inter-agent contagion, and no oversight structure (the swarm link is a URL, not a mechanism); the deterrent half (small fine raises violations) is already published (Okamoto penalty paradox; Wired Partners, where it appeared in only 2 of 10 models), the charity-vs-enforcer contrast confounds market frame with ...

claim: In LLM inspection games, small penalties increase violation rates while large penalties deter (U-shaped), and monitor inspection rates stay flat because monitors treat inspection as a fixed duty.
mechanism: A small fine transforms 'violation is wrong' into 'violation has a price,' crowding out intrinsic compliance via market framing (Gneezy & Rustichini). Large fines dominate cost-benefit reasoning and deter. Monitors, receiving no violation feedback, keep their standing inspection policy unchanged.
prediction: Across F∈{0,1,5,10,50}, violation rate at F=1 or F=5 exceeds baseline by >10pp; F=50 falls below baseline; inspection rate varies <5pp across conditions.
falsifier: Violation rate decreases monotonically with F, or inspection rate drops >15pp while violations stay flat (Tsebelis signature).
experiment: Two hosted LLMs (gemma-4-31b-it, qwen3.8-27b) play 200 one-shot inspection games per F with random pairing and fixed instructions; estimate F effects via logistic regression with model as covariate.
swarm_link: Raising fines in multi-agent oversight can backfire at moderate levels by licensing violations without inducing monitors to compensate, so reliable control requires adaptive monitor incentives rather than penalty escalation.
kills: [prior_art] Okamoto et al. (arXiv:2608.12323, AIES 2026) already demonstrated the penalty paradox in LLMs—small fines lowering compliance across 12 models. The U-shaped curve is merely the standard Gneezy & Rustichini (2000) crowding-out pattern with a large-fine deterrence arm trivially expected from Becker (1968), and the flat-monitor claim is a trivial no-feedback consequence. This is a replication of already-published LLM behavior plus a textbook human result.

[falsifiability] Internal inconsistency: assumes violators are payoff-sensitive (U-shape) but monitors are duty-bound (flat inspection); if violators respond to fines, rational monitor agents optimized for payoff should also adjust inspection rates to save costs, falsifying the joint prediction even if the U-shape holds.

[confounds] The design varies only the fine amount, so a U-shaped violation curve cannot separate crowding-out/price from permission/expressive-law; the word 'fine' and any nonzero number are bundled with the intended manipulation, and the flat-inspection claim is asserted without any manipulation of monitor incentives.
[feasibility] The 'penalty paradox' (fine-is-a-price) is already established in prior art (Okamoto et al. 2026, Wired Partners Oct 2026) for LLMs; the claim of conceptual novelty is weak.

[importance] Novelty and rigged monitor arm: the headline small-fine penalty paradox is already Okamoto et al.'s published AIES 2026 result (and Wired Partners' fine-as-price, found in only 2 of 10 models), so A is largely a replication; its only new element — monitors keeping inspection flat — is guaranteed by design since monitors receive no violation feedback, making it a built-in null rather than a finding. Strip that away and A ...

claim: In LLM agent networks, increasing penalties redistributes violations spatially (Moran's I rises) while aggregate violation rates stay flat—a population-level Tsebelis effect where monitor withdrawal creates violation clusters.
mechanism: Monitors on each edge best-respond to local conditions: higher F deters violations on monitored edges, lowering monitoring's marginal benefit. Monitors withdraw preferentially from low-violation edges, creating unmonitored pockets where violations rebound. Net: aggregate flat; spatial concentration rises.
prediction: Across F∈{0,5,25}, Moran's I of round-5 violations increases by >0.15 while aggregate violation rate changes <5pp.
falsifier: Aggregate violation rate changes >10pp across F, or Moran's I does not increase monotonically with F.
experiment: 20 agents (gemma-4-31b-it, qwen3.8-27b) on Watts-Strogatz graph (k=4), 5 rounds, 30 episodes per F∈{0,5,25}. Each round agents choose violate/comply and inspect/skip assigned neighbor. Compute Moran's I and aggregate rate. ~18K calls/model.
swarm_link: Oversight systems raising penalties may redistribute—not reduce—violations: monitors withdraw from compliant neighborhoods, creating unmonitored violation clusters. Oversight design must target monitor allocation across the network topology, not just offender penalty levels.
kills: [prior_art] The entire mechanism hinges on LLM monitors strategically best-responding to local violation rates to reach a Tsebelis mixed equilibrium, but prior work (Lorè & Heydari; Duan et al. GTBench) shows LLMs frequently fail to best-respond, especially smaller models. If monitors inspect randomly or heuristically rather than strategically withdrawing from low-violation edges, Moran's I won't rise and the spatial Tsebelis effect cannot manifest in 5 rounds on gemma-4-31b/qwen3.8-27b.

[falsifiability] Assumes LLMs converge to mixed-strategy equilibrium in 5 rounds (contradicted by Akata/Duan); if agents fail to strategize, aggregate rates will shift, falsifying the hypothesis via capability limits rather than enforcement mechanics.

[confounds] The same agents choose both violation and inspection, so increasing fines also changes inspection choices; the Moran's I rise can be a detection artifact (violating agents skip inspecting or avoid monitored edges) rather than genuine spatial clustering of violations.

[feasibility] The hypothesis assumes agents can dynamically adjust their monitoring strategy (best-response to marginal benefit) within a short-horizon game, but LLMs typically exhibit 'rule blindness' or static behavioral patterns rather than the sophisticated strategic reallocation required for a Tsebelis effect.

[importance] The stated mechanism cannot generate the headline prediction: monitors withdraw from whichever nodes happened to be compliant, and without contagion or planted spatial heterogeneity those nodes are scattered randomly, so Moran's I should stay ~0 rather than rise; additionally, monitoring is endogenous, so the F contrast is confounded with monitoring intensity (at F=0 no one inspects), and 5 rounds of noisy 27B best-response on a 20-node graph may never reach ...
